content: 1. Rodriguez MI and Gaffield ME authored a resource on how women can use emergency contraceptive pills. This work is unpublished but available upon request. 2. A study by Glasier A, Cameron ST, Fine P, Logan SJ, Casale W, Van Horn J, and others compared ulipristal acetate (UPA) and levonorgestrel for emergency contraception. This randomized, non-inferiority trial and meta-analysis, published in The Lancet in 2010, demonstrated the effectiveness of UPA as an emergency contraceptive. 3. Fine P, Mathe H, Ginde S, Cullins V, Morfesis J, and Gainer E conducted research on the use of ulipristal acetate (UPA) for emergency contraception when taken 48–120 hours after intercourse. Their findings were published in Obstetrics & Gynecology in 2010. 4. Rodriguez MI, Godfrey EM, Warden M, and Curtis KM performed a systematic review on the prevention and management of nausea and vomiting associated with emergency contraception use. This review was published in Contraception in 2013. 5. Salcedo J, Rodriguez MI, Curtis KM, and Kapp N conducted a systematic review to determine when women can resume or initiate regular contraception after taking emergency contraceptive pills. This review was published in Contraception in 2013. 6. Among the 58 experts who contributed to this work, 14 declared interests related to contraception. The World Health Organization (WHO) Secretariat and the Guidelines Development Group (GDG) reviewed these declarations. Anna Glasier disclosed an academic conflict of interest significant enough to exclude her from deliberations and recommendations related to ulipristal acetate (UPA). 7. Specific declarations of interest include: Eliana Amaral received $100,000 from WHO to research the pericoital use of levonorgestrel-containing emergency contraceptive pills. Sharon Cameron’s research unit received funding from Pfizer Ltd (UK) for studies on self-administration of injectable contraceptives and from HRA Pharma (France) for a trial on UPA effectiveness. Cameron also serves as a paid consultant for Exelgyn’s European Advisory Board. Alison Edelman is a co-investigator in studies funded by the NIH, the Bill & Melinda Gates Foundation, and the Society of Family Planning. Her research unit receives ongoing funding from Merck Sharp & Dohme Ltd (MSD) and Bayer Healthcare for studies on contraceptive methods. Anna Glasier works with HRA Pharma on developing new emergency contraception methods and was the principal investigator of a trial that led to UPA’s marketing for emergency contraception. Glasier’s clinic received research funds, and she continues to advise HRA Pharma on regulatory approvals and emergency contraception effectiveness related to body weight. Olav Meirik received $5,000 from WHO in 2013 to conduct a survey on combined oral contraceptive use patterns and serves as an unpaid senior research associate with the Instituto Chileno de Medicina Reproductiva (ICMER). Carolyn Westhoff receives honoraria from Agile Therapeutics and serves on data safety and monitoring boards for MSD and Bayer Healthcare. Her research unit conducts studies on IUDs, injectable contraceptives, and oral contraceptive pills. Jean-Jacques Amy received €2,500 from MSD in 2013 to present at a scientific symposium and an annual stipend of €5,000 from the European Society of Contraception and Reproductive Health as editor-in-chief of its journal. Andy Gray works at CAPRISA, a research unit that receives donated antiretroviral medications and microbicide products for clinical trials. Philip Hannaford works in an academic department that previously received fees from oral contraceptive manufacturers for lectures on contraception. Chelsea Polis collaborated on a trial investigating the acceptability of a subcutaneous injectable contraceptive, with Pfizer donating the injectable units for the study. Regine Sitruk-Ware received €1,500 twice in four years from Bayer for lectures on nonhormonal contraceptive targets and €4,500 in 2014 from MSD for advising on progestin development. 8. Julie Williams, employed by the UK’s Medicines and Healthcare products Regulatory Agency (MHRA), served as the lead rapporteur for the European Medicines Agency (EMA) Article 31 referral on combined hormonal contraceptives (CHCs). This review assessed the risk of venous thromboembolism across different products and influenced updates to CHC product information. 9. The EMA’s Pharmacovigilance Risk Assessment Committee (PRAC) and the Committee on Medicinal Products for Human Use (CHMP) reviewed the findings, which were made publicly available and resulted in changes to CHC product information.
